/Issued 100 PM MST Fri Nov 27 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

Northwesterly flow aloft has brought another breezy to windy day 
over central and north-central MT while mountain precipitation 
develops along the Continental Divide and gradually expands 
eastward and increases in coverage as the afternoon progresses. A 
fast moving and deepening trough then dives southeastward out of 
BC/AB and brings a period of enhanced snow over central and 
southwest Montana tonight into early Saturday morning. This will 
be a rather quick hitting system, but there will be at least a 
short period of moderate to heavy snow, especially for the 
mountain passes along and south of I90. The primary area of 
precipitation still looks to be slightly out of phase with the 
colder air aloft, but frontogenesis supported by H700 temperatures
dropping to -10C and north/northwesterly flow around 20 kts will 
favor at least some of the precipitation lingering later into the 
morning. The snow quickly diminishes and ends heading towards the 
late morning hours, with transient ridging bringing a period of 
drier conditions for the remainder of Saturday into Sunday. 

A weak shortwave associated with a larger trough over the Pacific
then ejects eastward into the Northern Rockies and brings periods
of light mountain snow and spotty lower elevation rain, snow, and
even some mixed precipitation late Sunday into Monday. Snow will 
be most prevalent along the northern divide and over far southwest
MT, near the Centennial Mountains/West Yellowstone area, but even
here, snowfall amounts generally remain below the 1 to 2 inch 
range. Lower elevation precipitation will be much lighter and 
spottier in nature, although there may be some instances of 
freezing drizzle impacts over some of the river valleys and other 
wind protected central/southwest basins that happen to retain 
colder air during the morning hours of Monday and Tuesday. 

The aforementioned Pacific trough undergoes shearing and splitting
as it moves onshore and into the Northern Rockies Tuesday into
Wednesday. With most of this system’s energy staying well south of
the forecast area, continued light mostly mountain precipitation
and breezy to locally windy conditions are in the forecast heading
towards the mid-week period. A moderately active west to northwest
flow aloft will maintain general unsettled conditions and near
average temperatures for much of the remaining week. - RCG

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

A quick round of accumulating snow over central and southwest 
Montana tonight into Saturday morning.

Wet mountain snow and valley rain showers will become more 
widespread by this evening in advance of the approaching trough, 
with snow levels dropping to the valley’s/plain’s floor by the 
late overnight hours into Saturday morning. The NBM 50th 
percentile for snowfall easily supports a general 2 to 6 inch 
range snowfall for the central and southwest passes, highest along
and south of I90. The exception to this is over the 
Gallatin/Madison ranges where amounts will be closer to the 3 to 8
inch range at pass level with well over a foot for the higher 
peaks. Even though the precipitation and colder air aloft don’t 
look to be optimally aligned, the combination of frontogenetic 
banding and north to northwesterly upslope flow may extend 
precipitation for a longer period than what model guidance is 
suggesting. Some of the 12Z hires models have begun to buy into 
this trend with snow lingering to around 9 am and even beyond, 
rather than shutting things off quickly by 5 or 6 am, mostly for 
the Gallatin/Madison mountain areas. Moreover, some of the newer 
guidance has also increased snowfall amounts for southwestern 
areas while decreasing amounts up north, especially for areas 
north of the US highway 12 corridor. 

This roughly matches the favorable meteorological pattern for 
accumulating snow over the southwest. With this in mind, I have 
upgraded the winter weather advisory for zone 330 
(Madison/Gallatin Ranges) to a winter storm warning and added a 
winter weather advisory for the Gallatin Valley given forecast 
totals rising to the 2 to 5 inch range in the Bozeman area. The 
north/northwesterly upslope boosts confidence in this decision 
beyond the recent model support. I also added all zones along and 
south of I90 to the advisory area since rain and wet snow may 
result in flash freezing conditions. Otherwise, moisture levels 
are generally not as supportive of snow amounts beyond 1 to 2 
inches in these areas. Impacts for all areas look to be greatest 
during the early morning hours on Saturday when snowfall is near 
peak and the aforementioned wet surfaces become icy and flash 
freezing in some cases. - RCG
